title: Delineating Oxidation Aspects of an Additively Manufactured Nanoprecipitation-Strengthened Al<sub>0.2</sub>Co<sub>1.5</sub>CrFeNi<sub>1.5</sub>Ti<sub>0.3</sub> High-Entropy Alloy.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: An additively manufactured (likely laser powder bed fusion) high-entropy alloy of nominal composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, produced from gas-atomized powder. The as-built microstructure is an FCC matrix with cellular substructure and high dislocation density, then heat treated (solution + aging) to introduce nanometer-scale L12-type Ni3(Al,Ti) precipitates for nanoprecipitation strengthening; possible minor B2 ordering depending on heat treatment.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Isothermal and cyclic oxidation testing in air or dry oxygen between about 700 and 1000 C for tens to 100 hours, with thermogravimetric analysis to obtain mass-gain kinetics. Comparative conditions include as-built, homogenized, and aged states. Post-exposure characterization by XRD, SEM/EDS cross-sections, TEM of oxide/metal interface, and possibly XPS/SIMS for depth profiles; assessment of build orientation or HIP effects on oxidation may also be included.
recollection.structure: Guess: A duplex oxide scale forms: an outer (Ni,Co)(Cr,Fe)2O4 spinel intermixed with rutile TiO2, and an inner Cr2O3 layer with only discontinuous Al2O3 lenses. Beneath the scale, an internal oxidation zone contains fine Al2O3 and TiO2 particles; near-surface L12 precipitates dissolve or coarsen due to Al/Ti depletion. Oxidation proceeds preferentially along AM melt-pool cell boundaries, giving a ridged or networked scale morphology. Scale thickness ranges from roughly 2 to 10 micrometers depending on temperature and exposure time; a continuous alumina layer does not establish under the test conditions.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Oxidation is initially controlled by Cr-driven scale formation due to AM microsegregation (Cr-enriched cell walls) and high defect density, leading to rapid spinel/Cr2O3 growth via short-circuit diffusion. The Al content (0.2) is insufficient to sustain a continuous Al2O3 layer, so protective alumina does not form; Al instead contributes to localized internal oxidation. Ti strongly oxidizes to rutile (TiO2), which disrupts scale adherence and promotes spallation. Nanoprecipitates (L12 Ni3(Al,Ti)) serve as local reservoirs for Al/Ti that become depleted near the surface, altering partitioning and dissolving the precipitates. Homogenization reduces microsegregation and lowers oxidation rates; aging slightly increases Al activity in the matrix and improves alumina nucleation but not enough to form a continuous protective layer.
recollection.results: Guess: Parabolic oxidation kinetics at 800–900 C with kp on the order of 3×10^-12 g^2 cm^-4 s^-1 at 800 C and ~1×10^-11 g^2 cm^-4 s^-1 at 900 C; mass gains after 50 h approximately 0.8 mg cm^-2 (800 C) and 1.8 mg cm^-2 (900 C). Oxide scales 3–8 micrometers thick after 50–100 h depending on temperature. Cyclic oxidation shows 10–20% mass loss upon cooldown due to partial spallation tied to rutile and spinel formation. Compared to as-built, homogenized material reduces kp by ~40% and aged condition by ~20–30%, but no continuous Al2O3 layer is achieved; the alloy remains Cr/spinel controlled with internal oxidation of Al/Ti.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies oxidation testing of as-built versus aged AM material but invents homogenized/cyclic conditions and misses the specific 750°C/50 h aging treatment. Its oxide-scale description substantially matches the mixed/spinel outer scale, continuous Cr2O3-rich barrier, and discontinuous inner Al/Ti oxides. The central Cr2O3-controlled protection and inability to form continuous alumina are also correct, though several proposed effects are unsupported. All quantitative values are speculative and the claimed improvement from aging is opposite to the observed higher mass gain of the aged alloy.
